title: Trump's Competing Iran Frames Kept Credibility Risk in a Chronic State
description_short: Trump's Competing Iran Frames Kept Credibility Risk in a Chronic State
description_medium: AP's March 2026 chronology places Trump's earlier claim that Iran's nuclear sites had been destroyed beside renewed warnings about the program before the February strikes. It also records his shift from criticizing regime-change wars to suggesting regime change in Iran and urging Iranians to take over their government. The article traces those statements across June 2025, January 2026 and the opening of the war.
description_long: The Associated Press assembled statements from several points in Trump's Iran policy. On June 24, 2025, he said Iran's nuclear sites were “completely destroyed,” a description Pete Hegseth and the White House repeated the next day. Before the Feb. 28, 2026 strikes, Trump again warned about Iran's nuclear ambitions. AP also compared his longstanding criticism of regime-change wars with a June 2025 post suggesting regime change could be appropriate and his later call for Iranians to take over after U.S.-Israeli attacks. The chronology included his January threats over the killing of protesters and his later claim that Tehran had stopped planned executions, alongside outside reporting of a higher death toll. Across those episodes, Trump's public language moved between claims of success, renewed warnings and calls for political change. AP documents that sequence but does not establish why he changed his statements or show that each comment reflected a new military order.

title: Lawmakers Move to Ban DHS WRAP Restraints After Trump-Era Detention Abuses
description_short: Lawmakers Move to Ban DHS WRAP Restraints After Trump-Era Detention Abuses
description_medium: Rep. Delia Ramirez introduced the Full-Body Restraint Prohibition Act on Feb. 25, 2026, after an AP investigation documented ICE use of WRAP devices on deportation flights. AP found a dozen local-law-enforcement cases in which autopsies linked the restraint to deaths; it could not establish how often ICE used it because DHS was not tracking or reporting use. The linked article gives the bill's provisions at introduction, not its later legislative status.
description_long: The Full-Body Restraint Prohibition Act, introduced by Rep. Delia Ramirez on Feb. 25, 2026, would bar the Department of Homeland Security from buying or using WRAP full-body restraints and require oversight and reporting. Ramirez cited an Associated Press investigation that found Immigration and Customs Enforcement had used the device on deportation flights since 2020, sometimes restraining people for hours. AP identified a dozen cases over the prior decade in which autopsies found that local law enforcement's use of the restraint contributed to a person's death. DHS was not tracking ICE's use as required for force reporting, so AP could not establish how many detainees had been restrained. The bill addressed concerns about prolonged restraint and limited oversight. Its introduction does not show that it became law or changed agency practice, and the linked report does not describe its progress through Congress after it was introduced.
subcategory: Indefinite Detention and Due Process Suspension

title: Dinner with Nick Fuentes - Dining with Holocaust Deniers
description_short: Trump hosted dinner at Mar-a-Lago with Nick Fuentes, a prominent white supremacist and Holocaust denier
description_medium: Donald Trump met Ye, formerly Kanye West, at Mar-a-Lago on Nov. 22, 2022, after Ye arrived with Nick Fuentes and two other guests. NBC reported that Ye asked Trump to be his running mate and that the conversation included politics and Ye's former wife, Kim Kardashian. Trump later said he had not known Fuentes would attend, and Fuentes backed that account. The report does not establish Trump's prior knowledge or identify every person present.
description_long: Donald Trump met Ye, the rapper formerly known as Kanye West, for dinner at Mar-a-Lago on Nov. 22, 2022. NBC reported that Ye brought three guests: Nick Fuentes, a white nationalist and Holocaust denier; Florida political operative Karen Giorno; and an unnamed parent of a student at Ye's Donda Academy. People familiar with the conversation said Ye asked Trump to be his running mate and discussed politics, including Jan. 6; Fuentes praised Trump and criticized Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis. Trump reportedly criticized Ye's former wife, Kim Kardashian. Trump later said he did not know Fuentes or his background, and Fuentes confirmed that Trump did not know he would attend. NBC reported that Trump had been speaking privately with Ye for weeks, but that does not establish what Trump knew about Ye's guests beforehand. The report identifies the three guests Ye brought, but not every person who may have been in the club's dining area. The conversation and prior-knowledge account remain attributed to sources and the participants rather than a complete attendee record.

preserved_fields.description_short: Trump hosted dinner at Mar-a-Lago with Nick Fuentes, a prominent white supremacist and Holocaust denier

title: Trump: Senate committee advances Trump's nominee for public lands chief
description_short: Trump: Senate committee advances Trump's nominee for public lands chief
description_medium: Senate committee advances Trump's nominee for public lands chief. President Trump's controversial nominee to lead the nation's largest public lands agency faces an initial confirmation vote Wednesday as Democrats point to his past support to sell federal lands. This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, or policy consequence linked directly to Trump. The downstream effects include elevated institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and measurable accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long: The Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee advanced Steve Pearce's nomination to lead the Bureau of Land Management on March 4, 2026, by an 11–9 party-line vote. Pearce, a former New Mexico congressman, had supported selling some federal lands and opposed national monument designations, positions that drew scrutiny during his confirmation process. At his hearing, Pearce said those views were in the past and that large-scale land sales were for Congress, not the agency, to decide. The committee's vote sent the nomination to the full Senate but did not confirm him. The hearing focused on how Pearce might manage the federal lands overseen by the bureau and whether his earlier positions would shape its approach under Trump. The record documents the committee vote and Pearce's answer about land sales; it does not show a completed change to federal land policy.

title: Trump Follows His Gut. His National Security Advisers Try to Keep Up.
description_short: Trump Follows His Gut. His National Security Advisers Try to Keep Up.
description_medium: Trump Follows His Gut. His National Security Advisers Try to Keep Up.. Decisions come fast, even if contradictions and inconsistencies abound. But without much of a process, there is little preparation for how things can go wrong. This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, or policy consequence linked directly to Trump. The downstream effects include elevated institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and measurable accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long: The New York Times reported that Trump relied heavily on personal instinct in deciding to attack Iran and that his administration gave changing public explanations. Trump told German Chancellor Friedrich Merz that he believed Iran would strike first. A day earlier, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the United States joined the operation because Israel was preparing to act, then tried to clarify his remarks. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt later said Trump had a “good feeling” Iran would threaten U.S. interests. The report also described a reduced national-security process: the National Security Council staff had been cut by at least two-thirds, and former aides said decisions were being handled by a smaller group with less formal option-setting. Those accounts raised questions about contingency planning as the conflict widened and casualties and economic risks grew. The article documents the staffing reduction and conflicting explanations; it does not show that a particular adviser could have prevented the attack or tie a specific outcome to the smaller staff.

title: Record Deaths in Immigration Custody Kept Mounting Under Trump's System
description_short: Record Deaths in Immigration Custody Kept Mounting Under Trump's System
description_medium: The Guardian reported record deaths in U.S. immigration custody amid complaints of poor care, opaque investigations, and a bureaucracy built to swallow accountability. This is what happens when cruelty gets institutionalized and then explained away with paperwork. The archive has to count these stories because detention deaths are not background conditions; they are the moral output of the system Trump keeps hardening.
description_long: At least 48 people died in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody after Trump returned to office in January 2025, according to reporting by The Guardian and NPR. Twenty-nine deaths occurred in the fiscal year that began Oct. 1, 2025, exceeding the previous annual high of 28 in 2004. The reports described deaths at the Adelanto facility in California and Camp East Montana in Texas and cited medical reviews documenting delayed or denied emergency care, misdiagnoses and inadequate monitoring of chronic conditions. In one Camp East Montana case, a medical examiner ruled the death a homicide after a struggle with guards, while early agency accounts described suicide or medical distress. ICE said detainees receive medical screening and round-the-clock care; advocates and medical experts raised concerns about overcrowding, staffing and oversight. The investigations document specific cases and disputed agency explanations. The overall count establishes an elevated number of deaths but does not by itself determine the cause of every death in custody.
